subject: physics
title: Particle accelerators and detectors
key_idea: Electric fields accelerate charged particles and magnetic fields bend their paths. Linacs and cyclotrons use both to reach high energies. A charged particle in a magnetic field moves in a circle of radius r = p / BQ. High energies are needed to probe nucleons and to create new particles.

blocks.text: Electrons for an accelerator are released from a heated metal and then accelerated by a potential difference.

items.meaning: The release of electrons from the surface of a heated metal, because the heat gives them enough energy to escape.

items: A hot filament releases electrons.
A potential difference between the filament and a second electrode accelerates them.
The electrons gain kinetic energy equal to the work done by the electric field.
A magnetic field applied sideways deflects the beam, because the force is at right angles to the motion.

blocks.label: Energy gained from a potential difference

items: Heated metal releases electrons by thermionic emission.
A potential difference accelerates charged particles. A magnetic field deflects them.

sections.heading: Linacs, cyclotrons and r = p / BQ

blocks.text: A charged particle moving at right angles to a magnetic field feels a force at right angles to its velocity, so it travels in a circle.

blocks.label: Radius of the circular path
where: p = momentum of the particle, mv (kg m/s)

items.text: The magnetic force is BQv. It is the centripetal force, mv² / r.

blocks.text: A greater momentum gives a larger radius. A stronger field gives a smaller radius.

diagram.alt: A practice calculation. Find the radius of the circular path of a charged particle in a magnetic field using r = p / BQ.
diagram.question: A particle with charge 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and momentum {a} × 10⁻²¹ kg m/s moves at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density {b} T. Calculate the radius of its path.

items: A line of hollow metal tubes (drift tubes) is joined to an alternating potential difference.
A particle is accelerated in each gap between tubes. Inside a tube there is no field, so it drifts at constant speed.
The polarity switches each time the particle is in a tube, so every gap speeds it up.
The tubes get longer along the line, because the speed rises while the time in each tube stays the same.
Two hollow D-shaped metal chambers (dees) sit in a vacuum, with a gap between them.
A uniform magnetic field at right angles to the dees bends the particles into semicircles.
An alternating potential difference across the gap speeds the particles up each time they cross.
Greater speed means a larger radius, so the path spirals outwards until the particles leave the edge.

diagram.alt: A sequencing activity. Put the steps of how a cyclotron accelerates a particle in order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps of one pass through a cyclotron in order.
steps: A particle is accelerated across the gap by the potential difference.
It enters a dee, where only the magnetic field acts on it.
The magnetic field bends it through a semicircle.
The potential difference reverses while it is in the dee.
It crosses the gap again and gains more speed.
The radius of its next semicircle is larger.

items: r = p / BQ comes from setting the magnetic force equal to the centripetal force.
A linac uses alternating potential difference across gaps between drift tubes.
A cyclotron uses a magnetic field to bend particles in semicircles between accelerating gaps.

blocks.text: Detectors show the paths of charged particles after a collision. This section covers how, and why such high energies are used.

items: A charged particle **ionises** the atoms it passes, leaving a trail that is detected.
A magnetic field **deflects** the particle, so the track curves.
The direction of the curve shows the sign of the charge.
The radius of the curve shows the momentum, from r = p / BQ.
Neutral particles leave no track.
To see detail, the de Broglie wavelength of the probe must be about as small as the object, and λ = h / p.
A very small wavelength needs a very large momentum, so a very high energy.
Firing high-energy electrons at nucleons shows that they contain smaller particles, the quarks.
High energy is also needed to create new, more massive particles, because E = mc².
Particles moving close to the speed of light live longer, as measured in the laboratory, than the same particles at rest.
This relativistic increase matters only when the speed is a large fraction of c.
It lets unstable particles travel further before they decay and be detected.
Relativistic equations are not needed.
Detectors use ionisation to show tracks and a magnetic field to curve them.
High energy means a short wavelength, which probes the structure of nucleons.
Fast particles last longer than the same particles at rest.

checks.q: Explain how electrons are produced and accelerated in a particle accelerator.
checks.a: A heated metal filament releases electrons by thermionic emission. A potential difference between the filament and another electrode accelerates them.

checks.q: Derive r = p / BQ for a charged particle moving at right angles to a magnetic field.
checks.a: The magnetic force BQv provides the centripetal force mv² / r. So BQv = mv² / r, giving r = mv / BQ = p / BQ.

checks.q: Explain why the drift tubes in a linac get longer along the accelerator.
checks.a: The particles speed up, but the potential difference alternates at a fixed frequency, so the time in each tube is the same. At a greater speed they cover a greater distance in that time, so the tubes must be longer.
